title: Where the data lives: choosing a database
hook: Relational, document, key-value, vector, graph and warehouse. The right home for each kind of ShopEase data.
inPlainWords: A database is where data is stored and asked for. Different shapes of data and different questions suit different kinds. Most AI projects start with one reliable source of truth, then add specialized stores only where they help.

useCase.title: Four kinds of ShopEase data need a home
useCase.story: Orders and payments (must never be wrong). Chat sessions and saved memory (flexible and fast). Policy documents and their embeddings (found by meaning). Three years of history for ML training (huge, read in bulk).

approaches.name: Relational database (SQL)
approaches.what: Tables of rows and columns, linked by keys, with strict rules and safe transactions.
approaches.greatWhen: Orders, customers, payments. Anything that must be exact and consistent.
approaches.example: An orders table linked to a customers table.

approaches.name: Document database
approaches.what: Stores flexible records, like JSON documents, without a fixed table shape.
approaches.greatWhen: Chat logs, profiles and varied records.
approaches.avoidWhen: Complex reports that join many kinds of records.
approaches.example: A saved conversation with its messages and notes.

approaches.name: Key-value store or cache
approaches.what: Look up a value by its name, extremely fast.

approaches.name: Vector database or vector index
approaches.what: Stores embeddings and finds the closest matches by meaning.
approaches.avoidWhen: Exact records like orders. It is a search helper, not a source of truth.
approaches.example: Find the policy paragraphs closest in meaning to a question.

approaches.name: Graph database
approaches.what: Stores things and the links between them.
approaches.greatWhen: Questions about connections, like what works with what.
approaches.example: Product to accessory to compatible device.

approaches.name: Data warehouse or lake
approaches.what: A large copy of history arranged for analysis and training.
approaches.greatWhen: ML training and reports over years of data.
approaches.avoidWhen: Live apps that read and write one record at a time.
approaches.example: Three years of orders for training the return model.

challenge.question: Where should the order and payment data live as the source of truth?

options.why: It keeps exact records with strict rules, so a refund and a payment can never disagree.
It finds similar things. It is not built to keep exact, consistent facts.
Fast, but it is a shortcut to data, not the place the data is kept safe.
It can work, but you lose strict consistency between orders and payments.

bestCase.title: One trusted source of truth, with specialists added only where they help
bestCase.example: Orders and payments live in a relational database. Chat memory sits in a document store. A vector index, inside the relational database or in a managed vector store, holds embeddings that point back to policy documents. A warehouse copy feeds ML training every night.

worstCase.title: Everything in one vector database, or a new database for every feature
worstCase.example: Order data is copied into a vector store "for the chatbot". The copies drift out of date, refunds show the wrong status, and nobody knows which copy is right. Or the team adopts five databases for five small features and cannot run them all.

takeaway: Keep one source of truth for facts. Add specialized stores for search, memory and analytics, and point them back to it.
